clinicalPearls: A great mimic that presents with fever of unknown origin, neurological deficits, and skin lesions in the absence of a discrete mass or overt lymphadenopathy
Malignant large B-cells proliferate selectively within the lumina of small and medium blood vessels, causing occlusion and organ ischaemia
A Western pattern often features neurological and cutaneous disease, while an Asian variant is characterised by haemophagocytic syndrome, marrow involvement, hepatosplenomegaly, and cytopenias
Common laboratory clues include raised lactate dehydrogenase, elevated inflammatory markers, anaemia, and thrombocytopenia
Diagnosis frequently requires biopsy of clinically involved skin, or random skin and other tissue biopsies, because there is often nothing to image
Tumour cells are CD20-positive B-cells confined to vessel lumina, thought to lack the adhesion molecules needed for transmural migration
A high index of suspicion is essential, as many cases are only diagnosed at autopsy
reference.pathophysiology: Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma is a rare aggressive B-cell neoplasm in which malignant cells remain confined within the lumina of small vessels rather than forming tumour masses. The cells are thought to lack surface adhesion and homing molecules required to exit the vasculature, so they accumulate intraluminally and occlude capillaries, arterioles, and venules. This produces widespread microvascular obstruction and ischaemic dysfunction of affected organs, most often the central nervous system and skin, and in the Asian-type variant the marrow, liver, and spleen with an associated haemophagocytic syndrome. The absence of masses and lymphadenopathy accounts for the elusive, multisystem presentation.
additionalDifferentials: Central nervous system vasculitis or multi-infarct disease
Systemic vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa
Disseminated infection or fever of unknown origin from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy of suspicious lesions, or random skin biopsies, and biopsy of other clinically involved organs
Immunohistochemistry confirming intraluminal CD20-positive large B-cells
Bone marrow examination, particularly in the haemophagocytic variant
MRI of the brain and lactate dehydrogenase, which are often abnormal
Ferritin, triglycerides, and fibrinogen to assess for haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
PET-CT, which may show non-specific organ uptake, and staging investigations
redFlags: Rapidly progressive neurological deterioration or stroke-like episodes
Features of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with multi-organ failure
Unexplained progressive cytopenias with rising lactate dehydrogenase
Deteriorating organ function without an identifiable infective or vascular cause
reference.prognosis: Untreated disease is rapidly fatal, but prompt recognition and anthracycline-based combination immunochemotherapy, with central nervous system-directed treatment where appropriate, can achieve remission in a substantial proportion of patients.
pitfalls: Failing to consider the diagnosis in fever of unknown origin with neurological or cutaneous signs
Relying on imaging, which typically shows no mass
Not pursuing random or targeted skin biopsy when suspicion is high
Overlooking an accompanying haemophagocytic syndrome, especially in the Asian variant
references: Swerdlow SH et al. WHO monograph on lymphoid neoplasms
management: Confirm diagnosis with tissue, often via a blind skin biopsy, since imaging is typically unrevealing and treatment should not proceed without histologic confirmation
Consider bone marrow biopsy when a haemophagocytic variant is suspected
Treat with systemic chemoimmunotherapy as the backbone for essentially all patients, combining an anthracycline based regimen with rituximab
Add central nervous system directed prophylaxis for essentially all patients given the high risk of neurologic relapse, using intrathecal chemotherapy or high dose systemic methotrexate
For patients with secondary brain or spinal cord involvement at diagnosis, individualize therapy among intrathecal chemotherapy, systemic high dose methotrexate, and radiation to involved sites
Treat with curative intent combination therapy in fit patients, since there is no conventional anatomic staging system for this disease
Reserve surgery for diagnostic biopsy only, it has no therapeutic role
Use radiotherapy selectively for secondary CNS or spinal involvement rather than routinely in first line treatment

Identify and manage associated haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis when present, particularly in the Asian type variant, given its independent contribution to cytopenias, organ dysfunction, and early mortality
Provide transfusion support for anemia and thrombocytopenia during treatment
Provide tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis and infection prophylaxis during intensive immunochemotherapy
Monitor response and toxicity with serial lactate dehydrogenase, blood counts, and interval imaging, anticipating hematologic toxicity

For relapsed or refractory disease after first line therapy, refer to a haemato-oncology or lymphoma specialist center to consider intensified or transplant based approaches, including allogeneic transplant or CAR T-cell therapy in selected patients, on a case by case basis
Refer urgently to haemato-oncology whenever the diagnosis is suspected, and involve neurology or critical care early for neurologic symptoms or Asian type presentation with haemophagocytic features
